items.question: What do you see as the capabilities that still need further work for vision-language models to meet the demands of autonomous driving?
items.object: The capabilities needed for autonomous driving beyond existing vision-language models
items.answer: There are some unique properties of the problems we're solving. For example, our stack relies on really powerful spatial awareness of everything going on around you, but then you need to understand the world in 3D even better. Another thing you want to incorporate is very long memory over a scene. You need to reason often based on the history of several seconds or more; that can be a lot of frames. You need to think how to prevent hallucinations. All of this is still very much ripe for further work, even though we have these vision-language models.

items.question: Why did you need accurate 3D pose estimation in your work on Street View?
items.object: 3D pose estimation for Street View
items.answer: I used to work on Street View as well, on 3D pose estimation and 3D vision for Street View. As the vehicles used to drive around, we would reconstruct the world in 3D, align all the different trajectories of all the platforms. We didn't just have cars; we had snowmobiles, trucks, bikes, bicycles. Sometimes we would put a trike on a boat. We've done all kinds of things at the time. You had to have accurate pose so that when you navigate all these photos, the panorama in 3D needs to look good.

items.question: How do you assess Waymo’s safety performance compared with human drivers?
items.object: Waymo’s safety performance compared with human drivers
items.answer: The most recent update was at 50 million miles, and there we share statistics about our performance as we drove people for the first 50 million autonomous-driven miles. In these 50 million miles there are different groups of incidents ranked in terms of severity. The most severe we track are incidents in which an airbag was deployed. These are fairly serious, high-impact incidents, and we are over 80% safer than human drivers would perform, in our estimate, in the cities where we drive and the conditions we drive in. When we adjust for all of this, we find that we have, I think, 83% fewer crashes that result in airbag deployment than if humans drove these miles. That's a nontrivial amount, so given the miles, that's over 60 crashes that we have potentially eliminated by having Waymos drive this. The second category of incidents is ones where there was some kind of injury. That one, we're again 88.1% safer than an estimate of what human drivers would do, given our domain where we drive. The third class is ones that are actually police-reported—more minor incidents, but still often you can report them to police. That one, we have, I think, 68 or so—64% fewer than our estimate of what humans would do. These are significant improvements. Separately, we've had studies done by insurance companies, third parties, that also confirmed that in terms of property damage or injury claims, we are about 80% less than what humans would do for a comparable amount of driving. Swiss Re is a company, so this is another separate benchmark, not just our own benchmarking.

items.object: Remote human support for Waymo’s autonomous vehicles
items.answer: In terms of can an operator inspect the vehicle, I think that is possible, but it happens rarely. The fact that we've scaled to such amounts of vehicles and such scope means you're not going to do it if there's people watching over every vehicle all the time. That's just not a good product. What did you eliminate? You moved the driver to sit behind the workstation; that doesn't work. This is mostly in very rare cases. Also, just to be clear, the vehicles are not teleoperated. It's not like someone drives them remotely. In these cases, at most, occasionally a person can confirm something the vehicle wants to do, and usually the vehicle already needs to be stopped for this to happen.

items.question: How do you think about adapting advances in AI to Waymo’s autonomous driving stack?
items.object: Adapting advances in AI and model scaling to autonomous driving
items.answer: Generally, we look at the state of the art in machine learning and AI. Our team has tried to adapt the advances to our domain, and usually it has involved some creative adaptation. There are some unique properties of the problems we're solving, and traditionally we had to do adjustments or fairly creative adjustments of the techniques we see. Every two years or so, my experience in this space is there's big technological leaps, and a lot of them have to do with machine learning or AI. In this space you want to keep reinventing your stack. As these advances occur, you digest them; you want to be at the forefront and take the benefits. I think what's happened in the last two years, if anything, there is an even bigger jump than before with these multimodal large language models, with generally generative AI technology that spans multimedia, obviously images, video understanding, audio handling, all of these things. It's been a bit of a revolution, and we are keenly aware of the advances and have been exploring them for the benefit of our driver. We've engaged in understanding and leveraging the technologies, such as vision-language models, diffusion prediction for generative outputs that can include videos, but also generate driving scenes for testing. We have leveraged things like 3D reconstruction advances. There's a lot of very interesting new technologies: Gaussian splatting, before that NeRF. These kinds of technologies are also very interesting, and we've been working on them. Generally, recently there has been this trend to scale the models and train them on a lot of data, scaled architectures, over time adding reinforcement learning to target even better reasoning capabilities. We have been scaling our models for a while, and we've had transformer architectures for a while. If you see our publications, we had a few even externally published around 2021, 2022 with transformers, even before that for certain applications in perception. We have been on this trend, but I think what has changed more is just the understanding of how much more scale we can leverage. Now we have gone and scaled the models and evolved them beyond what normally we used to do before, and we have seen clear benefits from doing it.

items.question: What do you see as the value of adapting a pretrained multimodal model like Gemini to driving tasks, as you explored in EMMA?
items.object: EMMA and adapting Gemini to driving tasks
items.answer: We have even published a paper called EMMA last year, where we took a state-of-the-art multimodal large language model—what Gemini people like to call theirs—and tried to adapt it for driving tasks. We adapted it reasonably successfully; we got some very nice results on the driving tasks. This is the idea of converting trajectories into tokens and passing them through the VLM. The way it works mostly is: What does Gemini bring to you? It brings you world knowledge. It's pretrained on the internet and it's a large model, so it understands a lot of concepts already that you don't have to teach it directly with your own labels or data. Then you fine-tune it on your tasks. You bring your own data and your own tasks, and adapt it to do well, given all this knowledge it brought to the tasks that you find you need to do. Of course, you need to adjust a bunch of recipes. You need to make sure that the tasks are well represented in the Gemini inputs, that all the sensors are properly scaled, and the right data sets are created, and so on. But when you fine-tune it, it does a reasonable job actually on these tasks.

items.question: Where do you see vanilla vision-language models falling short of the requirements of an autonomous driving system?
items.object: Limitations of vanilla vision-language models for autonomous driving
items.answer: There are still limitations. For example, our stack relies on really powerful spatial awareness of everything going on around you. It's helpful for safety, but then you need to understand the world in 3D even better. We have additional sensors like lidar and radar that are really superb for contributing to 3D spatial awareness that you want to incorporate, which a vanilla Gemini model does not do. Another thing you want to incorporate is very long memory over a scene. You need to reason often based on the history of several seconds or more; that can be a lot of frames. You need to incorporate this memory somehow, maintain it somehow, structure it. You need to think how to prevent hallucinations. The model can predict things, but every once in a while, if you go to domains where it has not seen things, it can be wrong. You need to think, what are the ways? We have a lot of experience launching powerful machine learning in every part of our stack, but doing it in a way with the stack design that is built to also mitigate all these issues of falling off the data manifold, hallucinating, and so on. All of this is still very much ripe for further work, even though we have these vision-language models. We want their power. We want to bring external knowledge; the internet has a lot of knowledge when you pretrain it. There's a lot of value in having these kinds of pretrained components, and we also can benefit from some of the architectures and scale.

items.question: What do you find appealing about large vision-language models for perception?
items.object: Large vision-language models for perception
items.answer: Without us having to label all these concepts, you can directly bootstrap yourself. The other power of all these models is the more scaled they are, the larger they are, the better they generalize. If you see some new variant of the concepts you for some reason didn't label, that you need to handle, before you would have to label a lot of examples for the small model to really capture what those things are like. Then every new, particularly different-looking thing, you need to label more examples. Here for perception, mostly, I'm thinking as I'm describing now, the large models, like Gemini or a lot of these other external vision-language models, mostly understand what it is already. It's a big model, and it generalizes. It can see a trench in a whole bunch of conditions and know it's a trench. For the small models this is harder; it requires more bespoke engineering to ensure. items.question: How do you see the Waymo Foundation Model helping you scale autonomous driving?
items.object: Waymo Foundation Model and scaling autonomous driving
items.answer: There's this interesting limit: How far can you push scaling, and how much of this knowledge can you bring into our model, such that now we can get data from new cities, from new countries, from different software platforms? You can move the cameras; you can change the lidars on the vehicle over time, which we do. We have a sixth-generation driver that keeps evolving the sensor stack, which is then something to think about. With all these properties, the question is, can we have a model that just generalizes across all of these things? We want to scale to dozens of cities. We don't want to do that much bespoke work. The best way to scale a model is, let's try to scale it in the data center first. Remove constraints of real-time response, which is needed for safe driving; remove constraints even potentially to only see events as they unfold. Remove constraints on how much you can scale the model. How much understanding can you get out of this model? How much can you generalize? We have been pushing to understand this question. I think we have been aiming to build what we call this Waymo Foundation Model, which is not just the vanilla VLM adaptation, but we want to bring in all these capabilities I recently talked about that expand on a standard vision-language model, and build it large, build it in the data center, and see how much it can understand all the data that we see and collect. The better this does, the more straightforward it is. This model then acts as a teacher to the models in the car. You can distill it down, and of course you still need to do this with thoughtful design, ensuring that the onboard stack fits all the safety and latency constraints. But then this thing is just the source of knowledge that you can always ask, both to mine data and to understand data. There's a very interesting question: How far can you push it? The more you push it, the more you accelerate the scaling, or seamless scaling, of the service. We want to explore that. I think that's a very exciting direction and it's in tune with the time today. I think it's the age of these types of models, and it tackles one of the historically challenging aspects of autonomous vehicles, and that is generalizability.

items.question: How do you think experience in earlier cities changes the work needed to launch Waymo in a new city?
items.object: Generalization across cities in Waymo’s deployment process
items.answer: It's been a very much evolving process. The first time, say we did Phoenix, we did East Chandler first, which is a bit of a suburban area. Phoenix and suburban areas have one set of challenges. For example, in protected left turns on a freeway—well, not a freeway, but a reasonably high-speed road, 45 miles an hour, and then people speed, so it can be a lot higher—and it's really important how you can go in front of traffic going at such speed. There are a few other challenges there, but it took a while to sort out and make sure our system is robust. Then you go to San Francisco and see it's totally different. There are all these crowds and totally different behavior, and a big part of the city is a lot narrower streets. It's just a different urban scenario. There it took a while too. Then we go to Los Angeles, which somewhat combines the properties of suburban Phoenix. By then we had moved more to downtown Phoenix, and so on, so we had a bit more of a span, everything from a bit more suburban to urban to dense urban, and San Francisco. items.question: How do you think predicting future sensor data could help pretrain an autonomous-driving model?
items.object: Predicting future sensor data as pretraining for autonomous-driving models
items.answer:
There's this interesting question: you can learn in our domain to predict the future too. How do you pretrain large language models? You predict the next token in language. What can you do in our domain? You can predict what the sensors give you in the future. Imagine if you could tokenize your sensors. You can predict the next sensor token and the next sensor token. If a model is able to predict accurately how sensors look in the future, whether it's lidar or camera or radar, they need to learn a lot about the environment because it will actually capture all the knowledge in here and predict how things evolve. You can imagine how you will see them, and that's very powerful pretraining. This is equivalent to next-word prediction.

The issue is only, of course, a word can be tokenized in maybe 100,000 tokens or something to that effect, and then you're predicting a distribution over 100,000 discrete tokens. That's fairly straightforward. Now our sensors are higher resolution, they can be different modalities. For those, what's the vocabulary? How do you predict it? That opens a whole bunch of interesting questions. Do you need an autoregressive model? Do you need diffusion-type predictors? How do you set it up, or a mixture of those? What is effective? There's work in the space already in academia and industry trying to build what's called a world model. You're dreaming the futures in the world that you're modeling from your own sensors, and that can be useful to train large models. How to best build it is also a very fascinating question.

items.question: How do you think about predicting a driving trajectory as an output of Waymo’s EMMA vision-language model?

items.question: How do you weigh the value of predicting other road users’ motion against predicting the full future sensor stream when training a driving model?
items.object: The tradeoff between predicting agents’ motion and predicting future sensor data for autonomous driving
items.answer:
With sensors, it's essentially the environment that goes with how you drove. Instead of predicting just how you drove, imagine observing others and predicting how they drive next to you. A lot of the models do this already. We have a model called Motion LM, published maybe two years ago, and there's work showing how to turn motion into conversation. You can train the models with that level of abstraction. You say, I'm not just teaching a model to predict how I drove; I'm going to teach it also to predict the other people's motion tokens around us, and so you predict jointly how a whole group of them behave. That's a richer signal. You're teaching the model more things from every example, and they're highly topical. Now you're teaching it not only how I behaved, but how everyone else reacts to me and maybe how I would react to them. You're modeling what we call the joint distribution of at least some group of agents around us. That's a richer signal.

Now you imagine you go to sensors: that's maybe a very high-bandwidth, detailed variant of everything that happened before. You not only see the environment, not only changes because you did certain driving paths; it also changes because others reacted to you and changed their behavior relative to you. That's also reflected in the sensors. Beyond that, you need to think how everything actually changes appearance as you and how objects may look from the other side if you surround them, and how reflections may work, and how certain light intensity relates to the RGB pixels, because now you're dreaming the future of the environment in its full fidelity. There's an argument that it's a more grounded prediction, in that it's reflecting the actual environment that the sensors are intended for. It's the most high-bandwidth prediction you have. This is all the information you actually had about the future, which is your full sensor, and that's the most you could try to predict.

But then the issue is, are you overdoing it? Humans don't spend their time thinking how the tree looks from the other side when they drive. I don't have to think how the branches occlude each other from a different viewpoint or how the shadow will evolve on that pedestrian. I don't necessarily have to think about it. While there's a lot of knowledge inherent that the model can capture, not all of it is relevant to driving; some of it is. So there's this interesting tradeoff: do you really want to go all the way there? How much benefit are you going to get?

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between end-to-end training and modularity in an autonomous-driving system?
items.object: End-to-end training and modularity in autonomous-driving systems
items.answer:
On the practical side, we will take the thing that works best. That's what I would say. End-to-end in general is a bit of an overloaded topic. It's been made into a big issue by a lot of people. It's compelling in some environments, but let's disentangle what end-to-end means. There's a mild definition and a strong definition. The strong definition is: you're going to pass some gradients from sensors to controls, what you want something to do, through a whole system, maybe to the sensors, and along the way learn features that you may not necessarily be able to inspect yourself, or that have semantic meaning, that just emerge from the training process and may help you drive.

End-to-end in general is a training strategy. It is orthogonal to where you have modules in the stack. You can still have modules and train things end-to-end if the models are connected properly and you can pass gradients between them. You can still train many tasks end-to-end. It doesn't have to be sensors to control; you can even potentially consolidate large pieces of the stack, so every piece of your stack becomes more end-to-end. Initially you had 10 different bespoke models handling certain tasks and now you consolidated them; that part became more end-to-end. It's a complex topic.

What we've learned over time is that you want few large components, if possible. It simplifies development, allows you to essentially scale those components more and optimize them, as opposed to having a bunch of little custom things each doing different stuff with different data generation. You want few consolidated components. Now the question is how few, and the other part is if you have a few, you still ideally want to backpropagate through them.

items.question: How do you assess the appeal and practical viability of a single end-to-end sensors-to-controls model for fully autonomous driving?
items.object: A single end-to-end sensors-to-controls model for fully autonomous driving
items.answer:
Sensors to controls is what people are really excited about in academia, and it's very powerful in an academic setting. It's a compelling idea: just collect enough data, you've got some black box in the middle that has sufficient scale or number of parameters, and you've got some desired output, and you let the middle part figure it out. Our EMMA paper does this too. We do train it end-to-end, and it predicts nice trajectories and generally does a good job with a fairly straightforward recipe. That's appealing.

But the big questions are: can you simulate and prove that this system does not hallucinate, does not do something bad, and that you can control it, introspect it, validate the system? Now I need a simulator that's always from sensors to controls, and in our domain there are quite a lot of sensors and they're not that easy to simulate. The technology for this has been evolving, and then you're really tied to this. You need to scale it. Imagine driving over a million miles a day in the simulator and having to simulate everything you could possibly see in these sensors. Most companies have at least a couple of different sensors, and you need to do a million miles with over a dozen cameras, a few lidars, and a radar, for example, and it needs to be really realistic. Otherwise it doesn't count. How do you do it? That's the challenge. How do you prove to yourself that all these cases can be validated just with this setup? That's hard.

Let's say you train a huge model and now you want to change it. What do you do? The only thing you can do is change the data to retrain the model. Now you fixed it, but maybe it broke something else. It's really hard to fix something really quickly. All you have is a model that goes into this. There are all these considerations.

I would say there is reasonable consensus in our space that you need few large components, but there is no consensus yet if it should be one component. I think a lot of it comes from the stability. When we're doing fully autonomous driving, it's top of mind. You design your stack in a way that you're sure you can test. That's a constraint. We need to do anything with the mindset that we actually know how to test this at scale to deploy a driver. When you're doing driver assist, it's less demanding; you don't have to test it to this extent. Maybe there you can get by with a fully end-to-end model, as some people have. But in autonomous driving, when you have to release it to drive hundreds of thousands of trips and millions of miles a week, that's a high bar. Between that and the ability to fix things as they arise, these are top of mind when you build a stack. With fully end-to-end, you need to have an answer. I think it's appealing to do end-to-end generally; it learns good features when you can do it. You just have to prove to yourself you can validate it.

items.question: How do you think about the safeguards needed to detect and control hallucinations in a large autonomous-driving model?
items.object: Harnesses for detecting and controlling hallucinations in autonomous-driving models
items.answer: If we have a model and it's some big VLM, even, or whatever, like we did with EMMA, we want to have a way to detect and steer it when it's doing wrong things and hallucinating. items.question: Why do you see testing an autonomous-driving model as scaling differently from improving its driving with more data?
items.object: The scalability of testing autonomous-driving models versus improving them with data
items.answer: There's this other interesting aspect of the simulator: as we collect more data and make our model larger, we can have it predict better trajectories for us. It's very data-efficient if we just want to improve over time and we get more data; we can keep adding data and the model will improve in certain ways. When we want to test it, we cannot do that. We need to think of all the cases that could go wrong and create some ways to validate all of those. They can require all kinds of hardware failures, sensors going wrong, rare cases; you name it, we need to handle all of this in our release cycle. That does not work as well as just taking data and feeding it to the simulator. The simulator tests us better, but it's not sufficient. We need to be very thoughtful on the testing side. It's not purely a data-driven exercise. We need experts thinking what could go wrong and working on mitigating that. It scales less straightforwardly than something where we can just put data in and the driver would improve with more and better data, suitably picked. That is true, but our ability to test it is not similarly scalable.

items.answer: I think you need to be very comprehensive. That's why it's hard to do just as some data-driven model that you just throw data into and somehow it tests you. items.question: What do you consider important about Waymo's safety framework for validating releases of its self-driving system?
items.object: Waymo's safety framework and release validation cycle
items.answer: We have published our safety framework. We are one of the fewer companies that have done it, and that details the whole set of tests we subject our driver to when we want to release it. It's a very broad set. It includes both kinds of hardware testing and failure injection, all kinds of standard analysis techniques, simulation, driving in closed courses, and testing with drivers and all kinds of things. This is actually difficult to develop. It's very comprehensive and takes a lot of effort, but we have shown that we can iterate over time and release improvements to our stack while going through this validation cycle. I think that's one of our great things we've been able to accomplish. It's bespoke, it's diverse, many things are combined. If you ask me what are we testing for, you need to test for a lot of things. One obvious one is you should feel you can be safer than the human driver. The second one is you should be confident you don't get stuck all over the place. The third one is you want to be thoughtful and mindful around, say, ambulances and police vehicles. It goes on and on. The amount of things you need to be able to do is broad. In construction, for example, or if directed by an official with some gesture, you need to try to understand it. It's a broad set of cases you need to check.

items.question: What do you see as the limitations of traditional computer graphics simulation for validating autonomous driving?
items.object: Computer graphics simulation for validating autonomous driving
items.answer: So far I was trying to tell you validation is difficult to scale. It's complicated. You need to handle all kinds of individualities, and some of them need experts. It's true, but the best way, or one of the best ways, to scale validation is still to use machine learning to build the simulator better, because the simulator is one big part of your validation story. Now you need realistic scenarios and interesting scenarios to be played in this simulator. Traditionally, maybe 10 years ago when I started, the state of the art in simulation was computer graphics methods. You collect a whole bunch of assets—houses and trees and whatever, bollards—and then when you drove it, you understand those assets, where they are and how they look, and then you just replace them with the assets. You place them there automatically, ideally, and then you have a world, a 3D world. Now you can drive in the 3D world and use computer graphics technology to make it look real. There was an issue where the models wouldn't react to the graphical versions of the things in the same way that they'd react to the real-world versions of the things. This is still true in a lot of robotics. They're correlated; they look similarish, but they're not the same. Computer graphics is a certain approximation, and who has the properties of what the sun should be like, and what are the diffusion aspects of the environment, and is there fog? You need to set a whole bunch of knobs properly. What is the camera? Is it detailed? Is it grimy or not? You somehow need all of this. It's really hard in the computer graphics environment. There are a lot of knobs, even though it's nominally powerful. Then there's this gap. Also, how good are you at taking what you drove and placing all these assets? Did you have all the assets? If you place different assets or set the conditions differently, is that again the gap? You're not guaranteed you'll be able to reconstruct anything you drove. items.question: What is your vision for a scalable driving simulator built from a vehicle's own sensor data?
items.object: A scalable driving simulator reconstructed from vehicle sensors
items.answer: The dream of a scalable simulator is to be able to just reconstruct it from your own sensors. We have enough sensors; they're extremely rich. They're cameras and 3D sensors. You should be able to go a long way into just building yourself the simulator from what you drove. The dream, and that's something we work to enable, is any situation I drove with my car, I can build a simulation environment from. I may have to populate it with additional traffic suitably. That's where generative comes in. I may need to evolve it in response to the things I do, because my decisions impact the decisions of others. They respond. I need to model that correctly; otherwise you're not going to have realistic outcomes. If the agent drove like what it drove when you weren't in front of it, it will plow into you, just because you did it. You can't just replay what the agents did and get all the signal you wanted. You need intelligent agents too. Between reconstructing the world and being able to drive, say, this intersection in San Francisco, and being able to populate it with agents that behave like it is reasonable for pedestrians and vehicles to behave, that's a really interesting, challenging machine learning problem. I'm inspired by this; it's fascinating.

items.question: How do you see the complementary roles of 3D Gaussian splats, NeRF, and diffusion models in building driving simulations?
items.object: The complementary roles of 3D Gaussian splats, NeRF, and diffusion models in driving simulation
items.answer: Some of these technologies—3D Gaussian splats, NeRF—for the reconstructive side of things, you can reconstruct a really well-represented version of the environment you drove. But those technologies don't necessarily allow you to augment it or dream it, turn day into night, or place new agents so easily. Something like a diffusion model is more of a generative type of model. It can dream new parts of the environment or agent behaviors, a complex one where the appearance matters or futures. But do you dream free-form, or do you want to condition yourself and land yourself at some specific intersection in San Francisco? How do you do the two together? There are some interesting questions here that I think the field is now making progress on. It's exciting, and we are alongside the field, making some exciting progress.

items.question: What kinds of problems do you consider worth posing to the academic community through Waymo’s research challenges?
items.object: Waymo’s research challenges for the academic community
items.answer: In parallel with data set work, we organize challenges on tasks which we believe are exciting and have headroom to make more progress in terms of interesting approaches and solutions. One of the interesting ones we're aiming to launch that relates to our conversation today a bit is end-to-end driving from just camera inputs. We are sharing some very interesting scenarios among the ones Waymo has seen, and we want to see how people can take some of these large models and get them to generalize on reasonably rare conditions. That's exciting. We also have a simulated agents challenge. We're unique in running such a challenge. It's a very interesting problem where you're building agent models that populate the simulator, and we have ways to validate whether they're good models. We improved the metrics a bit this year. We have one on traffic generation, again something we discussed. Let's say I give you the road graph of an intersection. I want you to potentially populate it with realistic traffic, where the relevant positions, velocities, and behaviors are reasonable—not ad hoc. We have ways to measure how realistic a traffic scenario is, and we want to see what people can do. There's interaction modeling as well. That's a challenge we're bringing back with a bit improved metrics from maybe four years ago, when we last ran it, around when we last talked.
